title: Thảo luận nhóm chọn dự án môi trường
transcript:
A: Okay, so we've got two proposals for the environmental project, and we need to settle on one by Friday. Marcus, you wanted to start with the wetland?
B: Yes. The marsh behind the sports field has been neglected for years. My idea is to clear it, then record which birds come back. I reckoned we'd need about twenty volunteers, though Mr. Ortiz said fifteen would be plenty.
C: I like the ambition, but I'm not convinced it's realistic. The ground there floods every spring, so anything we build could be washed away. And we'd need permission from the city, which could take months.
B: Fair enough, but we wouldn't be building anything. That's the point. We'd just be removing trash and writing down what we see.
C: Although, doesn't that make it less impressive? The judges tend to reward projects with something tangible at the end.
A: That's a good point, Dana. Remind us what yours was?
C: A rooftop garden on the science building. It's visible, it's measurable, and the principal has already said he's open to it. The downside is the cost. I've heard estimates of around eight hundred dollars, maybe closer to a thousand once you add soil and drainage.
B: A thousand dollars is a lot to raise by the spring, and honestly, I'd worry it's the kind of project that looks great on opening day and then gets abandoned by the summer.
A: What if we combined them? Start with the marsh cleanup this term, since it costs almost nothing, and use the photos and bird records to support a garden application later?
C: I could live with that, as long as the garden isn't dropped completely.
B: And I'd be happy provided we organize the volunteers properly this time.
A: Then I'll draft a schedule tonight and we'll vote tomorrow.

The ground is too wet for anyone to work there.
It might not impress the judges because there is nothing tangible to show.
The city will certainly refuse permission.
questions.explanation: Dana nói dự án 'less impressive' vì ban giám khảo thích thứ 'tangible at the end'.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'It would need more than twenty volunteers.': Số tình nguyện viên là chuyện Marcus và thầy Ortiz bàn, Dana không lo về điều đó.
Sai — 'The ground is too wet for anyone to work there.': Dana lo về việc xây dựng bị lũ cuốn, nhưng khi Marcus nói không xây gì thì Dana không còn lo điều này.
Đúng — Dana nói dự án 'less impressive' vì ban giám khảo thích thứ 'tangible at the end'.
Sai — 'The city will certainly refuse permission.': Dana chỉ nói xin phép có thể mất nhiều tháng, không nói thành phố sẽ từ chối.

choiceExplanations: Sai — 'True': Chỉ Marcus nói hai mươi; thầy Ortiz cho rằng mười lăm là đủ.

title: Phỏng vấn chủ nhiệm câu lạc bộ thiên văn
transcript:
A: Today I'm joined by Arjun Nair, who runs the school astronomy club and has just won a regional prize for his sky photographs. Arjun, welcome.
B: Thanks for having me. Although I should say the prize was for a team entry, so it wasn't really just me.
A: Modest! Now, your photos were taken from the roof of the school, in the middle of town. Most people assume you need a remote mountain for that.
B: That's the common assumption, and it's partly true. Light pollution is a real obstacle. From the roof we can see maybe a few hundred stars on a good night, whereas in the countryside you'd see thousands. But the city does have one advantage: you can't beat the convenience. We meet right after school.
A: So how do you cope with the glare?
B: Filters help, and so does patience. We take dozens of short exposures and combine them on a laptop. Honestly, the hardest part isn't the software. It's persuading people to turn off their lights.
A: Persuading? How do you mean?
B: Last autumn we wrote to local stores asking them to switch off their signs after midnight. Only two agreed, which was disappointing, but one of them was the big bookstore on Main Street, so it did make a visible difference.
A: Do you think it's a losing battle?
B: I used to. Now I think it's slow rather than lost. People tend to care once they've actually looked through a telescope. We held an open evening in March and over a hundred people came.
A: And what's next for the team?
B: We're hoping to borrow a larger telescope from the university, though nothing's been confirmed. If that falls through, we'll carry on with what we have. It's never really been about the equipment.

title: Bài giảng ngắn về hiệu ứng giãn cách khi học
transcript:
A: Right, before we begin the review workshop, I want to challenge a habit most of you have. Many students believe the best way to prepare for a test is to read the same chapter again and again the night before. It feels productive. The material looks familiar, so you assume you know it. But familiarity and knowledge are not the same thing.
A: Research on memory has shown something rather different. When you revisit material after a gap, say a day, then a few days, then a week, you remember it far better than if you study for the same total time in one sitting. This is known as the spacing effect. The effort of pulling information back out of your head is exactly what strengthens it.
A: Now, I'm not saying cramming never works. If your test is tomorrow and you haven't opened the book, then of course you should study tonight. It will help you for a day or two. The trouble is that it fades quickly, and then you're starting from zero next term.
A: So here is what I'd like you to try. After today's lesson, close your notebooks and write down everything you remember, without peeking. It will feel uncomfortable, and that's the whole point. Check your notes afterwards and mark what you missed. Then repeat the exercise on Thursday, and again at the weekend.
B: Does it matter how long each session is?
A: Good question. Short sessions of around twenty minutes are fine. Consistency matters much more than length. I'd rather see you do twenty minutes three times than one exhausting hour.
B: And what about using flashcards?
A: They're excellent, provided you actually test yourself instead of just flipping through them.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's main point?
choices: Students should avoid studying before tests.
Long study sessions are always the most effective.
Revisiting material at spaced intervals works better than repeated last-minute reading.
Familiar material is the easiest to remember.
questions.explanation: A nói ôn lại sau những khoảng nghỉ cho kết quả tốt hơn học dồn cùng tổng thời gian ('the spacing effect').
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'Students should avoid studying before tests.': A chỉ phản đối cách học dồn đêm trước, không bảo đừng học.
Sai — 'Long study sessions are always the most effective.': A nói 'Consistency matters much more than length'.
Đúng — A nói ôn lại sau những khoảng nghỉ cho kết quả tốt hơn học dồn cùng tổng thời gian ('the spacing effect').
Sai — 'Familiar material is the easiest to remember.': A cảnh báo rằng cảm giác quen thuộc không đồng nghĩa với việc đã biết.

title: Thông báo thay đổi lịch buổi hòa nhạc
transcript:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for your attention. I have a few announcements about the winter concert, and I'm afraid some of the details have changed since the poster went up, so please listen carefully.
First, the date. The concert was originally planned for Thursday evening, but the main hall is now needed for a regional exam. So we have moved it to Friday, the same week. Please correct your calendars, and tell your parents, because several of them have already asked.
Second, the time. The doors will open at six thirty, as before, but the performance itself will begin at seven rather than seven fifteen, because the school choir has to leave early for a competition the next morning. Orchestra members, that means you need to be backstage by five forty-five, not six.
Third, tickets. Prices have not changed: five dollars for students and eight for adults. However, tickets bought at the door will cost two dollars more than those bought in advance, so I would encourage everyone to buy theirs from the office this week. Anyone who has already bought a ticket for Thursday does not need to do anything. Those tickets will be accepted on Friday.
Finally, a request. Our program includes a piece written by one of our own ninth graders, and she has asked that nobody take photographs during it, as she is rather nervous. I'd be grateful if you could pass that on. Between pieces, of course, you're welcome to take as many pictures as you like.
That's everything. If you have questions, see Mrs. Alvarez in the music room, not at the main office, because the office has no further information. Thank you.

title: Tranh luận lịch sự về máy tính cầm tay trong thi toán
transcript:
A: I'll be honest, I think banning calculators from the math exam is a step backwards. In the real world, nobody does long division by hand. We're being tested on a skill that technology made obsolete.
B: I see where you're coming from, but I'd say you're confusing two things. Nobody is suggesting that arithmetic is the point of the exam. The point is to see whether you understand what you're doing. If you can't estimate that forty-eight times fifty is roughly two thousand five hundred, you won't notice when the calculator gives you nonsense because you pressed the wrong key.
A: That's fair, though mistakes like that are exactly what a calculator exercise could teach us to catch. And frankly, I'd rather my teacher spent class time on problem-solving than on drilling multiplication tables.
B: Hold on, that's a false choice. You can do both. Mr. Hendricks lets us use calculators for the final section of every test, and we still practice mental math in the first ten minutes of each lesson. It works rather well, in my experience.
A: Hmm. I suppose that's a reasonable compromise, but it still doesn't answer my main objection. Exams create anxiety, and taking away a tool you've used all year feels unfair. People who are slower at arithmetic get penalized for something unrelated to understanding.
B: That's the strongest point you've made so far, and I'll concede it. If the exam is mostly about arithmetic, then it's badly designed. But then the solution is to redesign the questions, not to hand everyone a machine and pretend the problem has gone away.
A: Well, maybe we're not as far apart as I thought. I'd accept a ban on calculators if the questions were rewritten to test reasoning rather than speed.
B: That I could happily support.

Mental arithmetic is the only real math skill.

title: Hướng dẫn làm thùng ủ phân hữu cơ ở trường
transcript:
A: Okay, you've all agreed to start the composting scheme, so let me walk you through the setup. The bin goes behind the cafeteria, on bare soil rather than concrete, so worms and other creatures can get in from underneath.
B: Why not concrete? It'd be easier to clean.
A: True, but a compost heap needs drainage and living organisms. Concrete blocks both. Now, the secret is balance. You need two kinds of material: greens, like fruit peels, vegetable scraps and fresh grass, and browns, like dry leaves, torn cardboard and paper. A common beginner's mistake is to put in only greens. It turns into a smelly, wet mess within a week.
B: So what ratio should we aim for?
A: Roughly two parts brown to one part green, by volume. Don't worry about measuring exactly. If it smells bad, add browns. If it looks dry and nothing is happening, add greens and a little water.
B: Can we put in leftover meat from the cafeteria?
A: Please don't. Meat, dairy and oily food attract rats and take far too long to break down. That goes in the regular trash, I'm afraid.
B: How often do we turn it?
A: Every two weeks is enough. I originally said weekly, but that's for people in a hurry. Use a garden fork, and mix the outer layers into the middle.
B: And when will it be ready?

title: Bản tin về thư viện hạt giống
transcript:
Good evening. The town library in Maple Grove has opened an unusual new service this week: a seed library. Visitors can now borrow packets of vegetable and flower seeds for free, the way they would borrow a book. The only condition is that, at the end of the growing season, borrowers return some seeds from the plants they've grown, so the collection can keep expanding.
The idea came from librarian Carla Mendes, who first suggested it two years ago. At first the council turned her down, saying the shelf space was needed for computers. She tried again last spring, this time with letters of support from three local schools, and the council agreed. The seeds themselves were donated by a gardening club and several neighbors, so the project cost the library almost nothing beyond a wooden cabinet.
On opening day, about sixty packets were borrowed within the first two hours, which surprised even Ms. Mendes. She had expected perhaps twenty. Most popular were tomatoes and sunflowers, while beans, which she personally recommends for beginners, were far less in demand.
Not everyone is convinced. One local gardener told us that some varieties cross-pollinate, meaning the seeds you return may not grow into the same plant, and that beginners may be disappointed. Ms. Mendes accepts this, but says that is part of the learning. The library will run a free workshop on saving seeds next month, and it has asked for volunteers to help sort donations on Saturday mornings.
And now, the weather.

title: Podcast về chuyện làm nhiều việc cùng lúc
transcript:
A: Welcome back. Today's topic is one that many of us are quietly proud of: multitasking. Dr. Kovacs, you've called it a myth. Isn't that a bit strong?
B: Perhaps, but I'd stand by it, with a small caveat. What we call multitasking is really rapid switching. The brain isn't doing two demanding things at once, it's jumping between them, and every jump costs a little time and attention.
A: But surely some people are better at it than others?
B: That's what people believe. In studies, the ones who describe themselves as skilled multitaskers often perform worse than those who don't. Their confidence outruns their ability, which is a rather human flaw.
A: Are there any exceptions?
B: Yes, when one of the tasks is automatic. You can walk and chat, or fold laundry while listening to music, because walking and folding need almost no conscious thought. The trouble starts when both tasks demand attention, like writing an essay while answering messages.
A: I think a lot of teenagers would push back on that. They say they do homework with music and a chat window open and still get everything done.
B: And I wouldn't say they get nothing done. They finish, but it takes longer and the quality tends to suffer. The more worrying part is that they rarely notice. Each time you check your phone, it can take a while to regain your earlier level of focus.
A: So what's the advice?
B: Work in blocks. Twenty-five minutes with the phone in another room, then a short break. And be honest with yourself: if you enjoy the interruptions, that's a sign they're pulling you away from the task.

title: Phỏng vấn nhà thiết kế trò chơi đến thăm trường
transcript:
A: We're lucky to have Jonah Weiss, a game designer, visiting our school today. Jonah, I think students imagine your job is mostly playing games all day.
B: I wish! In fact I spend most of my time on spreadsheets and meetings. The playing part is maybe one afternoon a week, and even then it's testing for bugs, which is less fun than it sounds.
A: How did you start?
B: With a board game I made when I was thirteen, for my younger sister. It was terrible, honestly. The rules were so complicated that she gave up after ten minutes. But that's when I learned the most important lesson, which is that a game nobody can understand isn't a game.
A: Was it difficult to turn that into a career?
B: People assume you must be a great programmer. I'm not. I can code a little, but the real skill is empathy: imagining what a stranger will feel at minute five, and at minute fifty. My first studio project failed, actually. We spent two years on a game that players found boring after an hour.
A: Two years! What did you do?
B: We scrapped half of it and rebuilt around the one feature people loved, a simple puzzle with a time limit. The second version did far better. I'd say failure was the best teacher I had.
A: What advice would you give students who want to follow you?
B: Make small things, finish them, and show them to people who'll be honest. Don't wait until you have a brilliant idea. And please keep enjoying other things too, such as books, music and sports. The best ideas tend to come from outside games.

A: So, for the documentary about the school's history, we have until the end of March, and we should decide who does what. I've found out that the school opened in nineteen fifty-eight.

title: Bài giảng về đảo nhiệt đô thị
transcript:
A: Today we're looking at a phenomenon you've probably felt without knowing its name: the urban heat island. Put simply, cities tend to be warmer than the surrounding countryside, especially at night.
B: Is that because of cars and air conditioning?
A: Those contribute, but they're not the main reason. The bigger factor is the surfaces. Asphalt, concrete and dark roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly after sunset, so the city never fully cools down. Meanwhile, fields and forests lose heat faster, partly because plants release water vapor, which has a cooling effect.
B: So adding trees would help?
A: Yes, and that's why many cities are planting more of them. But it's not a simple fix. Trees take years to grow, and they need space, which is scarce downtown. Some cities paint roofs white instead, because pale surfaces reflect more sunlight. That works faster, but it doesn't give you shade or a pleasant place to sit.
B: Does it actually matter? A few degrees doesn't sound like much.
A: It matters more than you'd think. During a heat wave, those extra degrees at night prevent people from recovering, and older residents and young children are especially vulnerable. So it's a health issue, not just a comfort issue.
B: Could we measure it at school?
A: Absolutely, and I'd love that. I'd suggest taking temperature readings at the same time in the courtyard, the sports field and the park nearby, over several evenings. Even a cheap thermometer will do. If there's a big gap between them, that would make a lovely report.

questions.prompt: According to the speaker, what is the main cause of the urban heat island?
choices: Cars and air conditioners alone.
Surfaces that store heat during the day and release it slowly.
A lack of rain in cities.
Too many tall buildings blocking the wind.

title: Góp ý bộ phim ngắn của một bạn
transcript:
A: So that's the final cut, Ms. Reyes. I know the ending is a bit abrupt, but the deadline is tomorrow.
B: I thought the first half was great, honestly. The shot of the empty bus stop in the rain says more than any dialogue. But the middle dragged.
C: I'd agree with Tom on that, Noor, though I'd put it more diplomatically. Your instincts for images are excellent. The difficulty is that the story pauses for about five minutes while the grandfather explains his past, and the audience doesn't need it all spelled out.
A: I was worried about that. I wanted people to understand why he never speaks to his neighbor.
C: But we do understand, long before he says it. Remember the scene where he puts two cups on the table and then quietly puts one back? That's all we need.
B: Yes! That was my favorite moment. I'd cut the monologue to a minute.
A: Hmm. It took me two weekends to film that scene, so cutting it feels painful.
C: I understand. Every filmmaker feels that. But a good editor is someone who can throw away their own best work for the sake of the film.
A: You sound like my uncle. Okay, I'll try a shorter version tonight and see how it feels.
B: And the music?
C: Lovely, though it covers the dialogue in one place. Lower it a little around the three-minute mark. I'd also check the credits, because one name is spelled wrong.
A: Which one?
C: I'll point it out afterwards.

title: Podcast về giai đoạn chững lại khi học ngoại ngữ
transcript:
A: Today we're talking about something every language learner meets sooner or later: the plateau. You progress quickly for a year, and then suddenly it feels like nothing is improving. Ian, you teach adults and teenagers. Is it real?
B: It's real, but I'd describe it differently. Improvement doesn't stop; it becomes harder to see. At the beginning, every new word changes what you can say. Later you already know the common ones, so each extra word adds very little, and the progress hides in details like word choice, rhythm, and understanding jokes.
A: So what do people do wrong?
B: Two things, mainly. First, they keep doing exactly what worked before, such as memorizing lists, even though they now need to listen to real speech. Second, they compare themselves to native speakers, which is discouraging and, frankly, unfair.
A: What do you recommend?
B: Change the kind of practice. If you've mostly read, start listening to podcasts at normal speed and don't stop to look up every word. Record yourself talking for two minutes and compare it with a month ago. That's often the first time people realize they've improved.
A: Some learners think moving abroad is the only solution.
B: It helps, but I wouldn't call it the only one. I've had students reach a very high level without leaving their hometown, because they talked every day with a friend online. Others lived abroad for a year and never improved, because they only spoke their own language at home.
A: So the secret is?
B: Regular contact and being willing to sound foolish. Perfectionism is the biggest enemy of fluency.

title: Phỏng vấn dịch giả thơ
transcript:
A: My guest today translates poetry from Spanish into English, which many people would consider an impossible job. Rafael, is it really impossible?
B: Some days I agree. People say poetry is what gets lost in translation, and there's truth in that. If a poem depends on a pun or a rhyme, you rarely keep both the sound and the meaning.
A: So what do you give up?
B: It depends on the poem. Sometimes I give up the rhyme to keep the image, because the image is what stays in your head. Other times the rhythm matters more, so I'll change a word that's close in meaning but sounds better. I make these choices constantly, and I'm not always happy with them.
A: Do you ever disagree with the poet?
B: Occasionally, politely. One poet I worked with insisted that a line about the sea be translated literally. I thought it sounded awkward in English. We compromised, but I still wonder who was right.
A: Some say a translation can never be as good as the original.
B: I'm not sure that's the right question. A translation is a different poem written by a second person, using the first poem as a starting point. It may be worse, but it may also introduce readers to something they would never otherwise have read, and surely that counts for a lot.
A: What would you say to students who are learning a language?
B: Read poems in the original, even if you only understand half. Sounds carry feeling before meaning does. And then try translating a short one. It teaches you more about your own language than anything else I know.
